By Dr. Elena Rostova, M.P.H. Biostatistics & Health Metrics · Medically reviewed by Dr. Elena Rostova, M.P.H. on November 20, 2026 · Last updated: November 27, 2026

What BMI measures, and what it does not

Body Mass Index compares your weight with your height. It is a quick screening number used by doctors and public-health researchers to flag possible weight-related risk across large groups. It is not a diagnosis and it does not measure body fat directly. The calculator above gives you the number; this page helps you interpret it sensibly.

The formulas

  • Metric: BMI = weight (kg) ÷ height (m)²
  • Imperial: BMI = 703 × weight (lb) ÷ height (in)²

Example, metric: 70 kg at 175 cm. Height is 1.75 m, so BMI = 70 ÷ 3.0625 = 22.9. Example, imperial: 150 lb at 5 ft 7 in (67 in). BMI = 703 × 150 ÷ 4,489 = 23.5.

WHO adult categories

BMICategory
Below 18.5Underweight
18.5 to 24.9Normal range
25.0 to 29.9Overweight (pre-obese)
30.0 to 34.9Obesity class I
35.0 to 39.9Obesity class II
40.0 and aboveObesity class III

Your healthy weight range by height

Reverse the formula to find the weight range that corresponds to a BMI of 18.5 to 24.9: weight = BMI × height². For a person who is 175 cm tall, that is 18.5 × 3.0625 = 56.7 kg up to 24.9 × 3.0625 = 76.3 kg. At 160 cm the range is 47.4 kg to 63.7 kg. Notice that the range is wide: roughly 20 kg for an average-height adult. Being at one end or the other is not automatically better, and age, sex, muscle and frame all matter.

Why the standard cut-offs do not fit everyone

South and East Asian adults. Studies show that people of Asian descent often carry more body fat and higher metabolic risk at a lower BMI. A WHO expert consultation recommended additional action points at 23 and 27.5, and several Indian clinical guidelines use 23 as the start of "overweight" and 25 as "obese". For a 175 cm adult, a BMI of 23 corresponds to about 70 kg, compared with about 76 kg for a BMI of 25. If you are of Asian origin, discuss which thresholds your doctor uses.

Athletes and muscular people. Muscle weighs more than fat for the same volume. A strength athlete weighing 100 kg at 180 cm has a BMI of 30.9, which falls in "obesity class I", despite a low body-fat percentage. For them BMI is the wrong tool.

Older adults. People lose muscle and height with age. A "normal" BMI can hide low muscle mass, and some research suggests a slightly higher BMI in later life is not as harmful as in middle age. This is a conversation for a clinician.

Children, teenagers and pregnancy. The adult table does not apply. Children's BMI is compared with age- and sex-specific growth charts, and pregnancy changes weight for good reasons. Use a paediatric or antenatal tool or ask your doctor.

Measurements that add information

  • Waist circumference. Fat around the abdomen is linked to higher health risk. A tape measure at the navel level takes seconds.
  • Waist-to-height ratio. Keeping your waist under half your height is a common rule of thumb.
  • Blood pressure, blood sugar and cholesterol. These show how your body is actually doing, and no calculator can replace them.

What to do with your result

  • In the normal range: keep up regular activity and balanced eating. The number is not a goal to chase lower.
  • Above the range: consider waist measurement and a check-up. Gradual changes to activity, sleep and eating habits usually work better than crash diets.
  • Below the range: unintended weight loss or low weight is worth discussing with a doctor, who can check for nutritional or medical causes.

If you are worried about your relationship with food or your body, a BMI calculator is not the right place to look for answers. Speak with a doctor or a qualified mental health professional.

Common mistakes

  • Entering height in centimetres into the imperial formula, or inches into the metric one.
  • Treating 24.9 as healthy and 25.0 as unhealthy. The categories are conventions, not cliffs.
  • Using adult categories for a child.
  • Judging fitness on BMI alone.

Frequently asked questions

How do I calculate BMI manually?

Divide your weight in kilograms by your height in metres squared. In pounds and inches, multiply by 703 after dividing weight by height squared.

What is a healthy BMI?

The WHO normal range for adults is 18.5 to 24.9. For some Asian populations, lower action points of 23 and 27.5 are suggested.

Is BMI accurate for athletes?

Not usually. BMI does not separate muscle from fat, so muscular people can be classified as overweight or obese. Body fat percentage or waist measurements give a better picture.

Does BMI apply to children?

No. Children's BMI is interpreted using percentiles for their age and sex, and should be reviewed by a paediatrician.

Methodology and sources

Categories follow the World Health Organization's adult BMI classification. See the WHO BMI page for the reference definitions. This tool is educational and is not medical advice or a diagnosis.
